411.event_title: Charlemagne learns by listening at his court
411.event: According to his courtier and biographer Einhard, Charlemagne had books read aloud to him at meals, especially histories and Augustine's City of God, and took lessons in rhetoric, logic and astronomy from the English scholar Alcuin of York, whom he invited around 781 to lead the circle of learning at his court. Einhard also records that the emperor tried to learn to write late in life, keeping writing tablets under his pillow, but with little success. Charlemagne's patronage of scholars helped launch the revival of learning known as the Carolingian Renaissance.
411.explanation: The ruler of the largest Western empire since Rome, who never mastered writing, acquired wide learning chiefly through his ears and made the pursuit of learning a priority of his reign.
411.tie_back: The kural calls the wealth gained through the ear the foremost of all riches, and Charlemagne, master of vast lands and treasure, built much of his knowledge on what he heard read and taught.
411._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of learning by hearing, though Einhard was an admiring biographer and Charlemagne also learned to read, so his knowledge did not come by ear alone.

412.event_title: Marie Sklodowska studies in Paris on a meagre diet
412.event: In the autumn of 1891 the young Polish student Maria Sklodowska, later Marie Curie, enrolled at the Sorbonne, and after a few months moved to a cold garret in the Latin Quarter to be close to the university. She had enough money for tuition, her room and the cheapest food, and by her own later account her meals were often reduced to bread with chocolate, eggs or fruit while she attended lectures and studied far into the night. Though she arrived less well prepared than her classmates, she finished first in the physics degree examinations in 1893 and second in mathematics in 1894.
412.explanation: Her student years are remembered as an example of someone who put instruction ahead of comfort and even of a proper diet.
412.tie_back: The kural says the stomach should be given only a little, when there is no food for the ear, and the young Sklodowska fed her mind on lectures and study while giving her body as little as she could manage.
412._accuracy_note: A good match for putting learning before food, but her frugality was driven partly by poverty, and much of her learning came from reading and laboratory work rather than from hearing alone.

413.event_title: UNESCO recognises the oral tradition of Vedic chanting
413.event: The Vedas, the oldest sacred texts of Hinduism, are classed as shruti, a Sanskrit word meaning what is heard, and were preserved for many centuries through memorisation and recitation before being written down. Their hymns and formulae were chanted at sacred rituals, including sacrifices, and reciters are trained from childhood in exact techniques of pitch accent, pronunciation and word combination so that the sound of every word stays unaltered. In 2008 UNESCO inscribed the Tradition of Vedic Chanting on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
413.explanation: The recognition honours one of the world's oldest bodies of knowledge, handed down for thousands of years almost entirely by ear and regarded by its tradition as sacred.
413.tie_back: The kural matches those who feed on the food of the ear with the gods who receive sacrificial oblations, and the Vedic tradition, learned by hearing and chanted at those very sacrifices, treats what is received through the ear as holy.
413._accuracy_note: Captures the kural's linking of hearing with sacrifice and sanctity, but it is the recognition of a tradition rather than an event showing hearers raised to the status of the gods.

414.event_title: Bookbinder's apprentice Michael Faraday attends Humphry Davy's lectures
414.event: Michael Faraday, who had been apprenticed to a London bookbinder at fourteen and had no university education, was given a ticket in 1812 to hear Humphry Davy's chemistry lectures at the Royal Institution. He took careful notes, bound them into a volume, and presented them to Davy in the hope of scientific work. On 1 March 1813 he was appointed laboratory assistant at the Royal Institution, the beginning of a career that made him one of the greatest experimental scientists of the nineteenth century.
414.explanation: A few lectures heard by a young tradesman opened the way to discoveries in electricity and magnetism that shaped the modern world.
414.tie_back: The kural urges those who have not studied to listen to the learned, since hearing will be a staff to them in adversity, and Faraday, without formal schooling, rose from the bookbinder's bench by listening to Davy.
414._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural, though Faraday also educated himself by reading the books he bound.

415.event_title: Augustine listens to the sermons of Ambrose in Milan
415.event: In the mid-380s Augustine, a gifted teacher of rhetoric from North Africa who had followed the Manichaean sect for years, took up a publicly paid professorship in Milan, then the imperial capital of the West. There he became a regular listener at the preaching of the city's bishop, Ambrose, whose allegorical method of interpreting Scripture helped remove his objections to Christianity. In the summer of 386 he gave up his professorship, and Ambrose baptised him at Easter 387.
415.explanation: The sermons of a respected bishop helped carry one of the most influential thinkers in Western history through a long period of doubt and indecision.
415.tie_back: The kural compares the words of upright people to a staff for one walking on slippery ground, and Ambrose's preaching gave the wavering Augustine something firm to lean on.
415._accuracy_note: A close fit, though Augustine was also moved by Neoplatonist writings and by friends, so Ambrose's words were one support among several.

416.event_title: Booker T. Washington overhears talk of Hampton Institute in a coal mine
416.event: As a teenager working in a coal mine near Malden, West Virginia, Booker T. Washington, who had been born into slavery, overheard two miners talking in the dark about a school in Virginia for Black students where poor students could work to pay for their board while learning a trade. After some months more in the mine and in domestic service, he set out for the Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute in the fall of 1872, arriving with only fifty cents. He graduated and went on to lead Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, becoming one of the most prominent educators in American history.
416.explanation: A few words overheard in a mine changed the course of a life and, through Tuskegee, the education of thousands.
416.tie_back: The kural says that listening to good things, however little, brings full greatness, and a single overheard conversation set Washington on the road to national prominence.
416._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of how even a little good hearing can lead to greatness, though it rests largely on Washington's own autobiography.

417.event_title: Kepler refuses to ignore an eight-minute error in the orbit of Mars
417.event: Working with Tycho Brahe's precise observations of Mars, Johannes Kepler spent years trying to account for the planet's motion with combinations of circles, as astronomers had done since antiquity. His best circular model still disagreed with Tycho's data by about eight minutes of arc, and because he trusted those observations to about two minutes, he would not accept it. Re-examining the problem from its foundations, he found that Mars moves in an ellipse, and published his first two laws of planetary motion in Astronomia Nova in 1609.
417.explanation: Kepler's refusal to let a near-miss stand turned a mistaken assumption into one of the great discoveries of science.
417.tie_back: The kural says those who have examined matters minutely will not speak foolishly even when they have misunderstood something, and Kepler's careful checking kept his early, mistaken model from becoming his published conclusion.
417._accuracy_note: Fits the kural's point that thorough examination keeps errors from becoming folly, but Kepler's learning came from study and observation rather than the hearing this chapter praises.

418.event: On 14 April 1912, during her maiden voyage, RMS Titanic received a series of wireless warnings from other ships about ice ahead; most were passed to the bridge, but a late message from the Mesaba reporting heavy pack ice and many large icebergs was never delivered because the operator was busy sending passengers' messages. The ship did not slow down, struck an iceberg shortly before midnight, and sank early on 15 April with the loss of more than 1,500 lives. The United States inquiry criticised the captain for failing to reduce speed after receiving ice warnings, and the disaster led to round-the-clock radio watches and the International Ice Patrol.
418.explanation: The disaster showed that warnings which are heard but not heeded give no protection.
418.tie_back: The kural says ears that have not been opened by instruction are as good as deaf even though they hear sounds, and the Titanic received warning after warning without letting them change its course or speed.
418._accuracy_note: Illustrates hearing without truly hearing, but the kural concerns a lifelong failure to be shaped by instruction, and responsibility for the disaster was shared and complex.

419.event_title: Gandhi spends a year listening before taking part in Indian politics
419.event: When Mohandas Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in January 1915, his political mentor Gopal Krishna Gokhale made him promise to spend a year travelling the country to gain experience, keeping his ears open and expressing no opinion on public questions until this period of probation was over. Gandhi kept the promise even after Gokhale died in February 1915, and spent much of the year touring India and meeting people of many regions and communities.
419.explanation: Gandhi's later ability to speak to and for India's very diverse people rested partly on this deliberate period of listening before speaking.
419.tie_back: The kural says that those without refined learning gained by hearing can hardly speak with humility, and Gokhale's counsel made Gandhi listen widely before he spoke, grounding his later public speech in what he had heard.
419._accuracy_note: A clear case of deliberate listening shaping restrained speech, though Gandhi was already experienced and widely respected, so the year refined rather than created his humility.

420.event_title: Crassus rejects advice before the Battle of Carrhae
420.event: Marcus Licinius Crassus, one of the richest men in Rome, led a Roman army against the Parthian Empire in 53 BCE. According to Plutarch, he turned down the Armenian king Artavasdes' advice to advance through the hills of Armenia, where Parthian cavalry would be less effective, and instead followed an Arab chieftain, Ariamnes, onto the open plains of Mesopotamia. Near Carrhae the Parthian horse archers under Surena defeated his army, and Crassus was killed soon afterwards.
420.explanation: The campaign became a classic warning of how a powerful man who would not listen to counsel could bring ruin on himself and his army.
420.tie_back: The kural dismisses those who know only the tastes of the mouth and never those of the ear, and Crassus, famous for his hunger for wealth, would not take in the advice that might have saved him.
420._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the kural condemns a whole life lived without cultivating the ear, while this is a single refusal of advice reported mainly by Plutarch.
